title: A Extraction for the Ghost
premise: Tamsin Brightwater, a whistle-blower living under four names after exposing a financial crimes syndicate, is contacted by a stranger who claims Tamsin once saved his life—a favor Tamsin has no memory of. The stranger, a fixer named Ilya Voss, demands repayment: help him stop a staged 'accident' at a Frankfurt trading hub that will wipe out evidence and lives before markets open. As Tamsin is dragged back into the world he fled, he discovers the favor was manufactured—Voss engineered the debt to recruit the one man who can crack the syndicate's encrypted ledger. In the end, Tamsin must choose between erasing himself forever and testifying under his real name, sacrificing his anonymity to stop the attack and finally own who he is.
about_author: Quentin Quintana is a former risk analyst who spent a decade inside the compliance departments of European banks before turning to fiction. He writes thrillers about people trapped by paperwork, and lives somewhere in Portugal under no particular name.

chapters.title: The Fourth Name
chapters.summary: Tamsin Brightwater's POV. Living quietly in Rotterdam as 'Daniel Vos,' Tamsin follows his rigid survival routines—cash, burner phones, no patterns. A letter arrives thanking him for a favor he never performed. The beat: unease cracking the shell of a carefully invisible life.

chapters.title: Interest Owed
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The stranger, Ilya Voss, appears at his workplace, calm and certain, detailing the supposed life-debt with unsettling precision. He gives Tamsin seventy-two hours to repay it: come to Brussels. The beat: dread—the rules that kept him safe are being rewritten in real time.

chapters.title: Rules of Disappearance
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with flashbacks to the whistle-blowing that forced him under four names five years ago. He weighs running again versus confronting Voss. His handler's dead-drop signals have gone silent. The beat: isolation deepening; the safety net was always thinner than he believed.

chapters.title: Brussels, Third Platform
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He meets Voss in a rail station crowd. Voss reveals the target: a coordinated 'accident'—a gas failure—at the EuroClear-style clearing house in Frankfurt, timed before markets open, designed to destroy records of the syndicate's trades. The beat: reluctant curiosity becoming compulsion.

chapters.title: A Debt That Never Was
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. We learn Voss fabricated the favor story—he needed leverage on the one analyst whose testimony could unlock the syndicate's ledger. But his motives are tangled: someone he loved died in an earlier 'accident.' The beat: moral ambiguity; the liar believes his lie.

chapters.title: Ledger of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Shown fragments of the encrypted ledger, Tamsin recognizes his own redactions from five years ago—the syndicate survived his whistle-blowing by burying it deeper. The beat: fury and vertigo; his sacrifice accomplished nothing.

chapters.title: Four Names, One Face
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Tamsin tests whether Voss knows his true identity or just his patterns. Meanwhile, a syndicate cleaner, Mara Kessler, picks up Tamsin's trail in Rotterdam through a routine bank slip. The beat: hunter and hunted converging.

chapters.title: The Handler's Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He travels to his old protection contact in Antwerp and finds the safe flat stripped and the contact gone—or worse. Evidence suggests the protection program itself was compromised from the start. The beat: betrayal; there was never anyone behind him.

chapters.title: Kessler
chapters.summary: Mara Kessler's POV. Coldly professional, she reconstructs Tamsin's four identities and reports upward—but her report triggers orders that make even her hesitate: eliminate everyone touched by the file. The beat: the machinery of the syndicate revealed as indifferent to its own tools.

chapters.title: Frankfurt Before Dawn
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Voss's POV, alternating. They scout the clearing house, mapping how the gas 'failure' will be staged and which insiders are bought. Tamsin spots a flaw in the plan—and realizes stopping it publicly would expose him. The beat: the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: What the Markets Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He decrypts a portion of the ledger using his old analyst skills and finds his own name listed not as a threat but as an asset—one the syndicate planned to 'recover.' The beat: horror reframed; he was never free, only deferred.

chapters.title: The Favor, Reversed
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Confronted by Tamsin about the fabricated debt, Voss admits it—but argues the lie produced a truth: Tamsin is the only person who can stop the attack. Their alliance fractures and reforms. The beat: loyalty vs. truth crystallized between two men built on false foundations.

chapters.title: Safe House Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Hiding with Voss, Tamsin calculates odds: warn authorities and trigger the attack early, or intervene quietly and stay hunted forever. Kessler closes in on their location. The beat: claustrophobic tension; every option costs something irreplaceable.

chapters.title: Breach
chapters.summary: Kessler's POV shifting to Tamsin's mid-chapter. Kessler raids the safe house; Voss is wounded covering Tamsin's escape. Tamsin flees with the ledger fragment—the only proof of the plot. The beat: guilt and adrenaline; the debt becomes real after all.

chapters.title: Confessions at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Tamsin and wounded Voss, hiding in a freight yard. Voss tells the truth about the woman he lost, and Tamsin confesses what whistle-blowing cost him—a brother who stopped answering, a self he abandoned. The beat: raw intimacy; two ghosts comparing hauntings.

chapters.title: The Insider
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Following the ledger, they identify the insider who'll trigger the gas release: a junior engineer being blackmailed. Tamsin sees his younger self in the man. The beat: empathy as strategy; turning the syndicate's pawn into their asset.

chapters.title: Ninety Minutes to Open
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. Pre-dawn Frankfurt: Kessler's team locks down the building, the engineer is positioned, and Tamsin infiltrates through service tunnels while Voss creates a diversion. The beat: ticking-clock escalation, every thread pulled taut.

chapters.title: Accident, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Climax: Tamsin reaches the valve room, convinces the engineer to stand down seconds before release, but Kessler arrives. Voss takes a fatal bullet buying Tamsin the moment to trigger the alarms—forcing an evacuation that makes the 'accident' impossible to stage. The beat: sacrifice repaying a debt that was never owed.

chapters.title: Markets Open
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The exchange opens normally; the world never knows what almost happened. Kessler escapes, and the syndicate begins burning its own records—unaware Tamsin holds the ledger fragment. The beat: hollow victory; survival without yet a self.

chapters.title: The Fifth Name
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Offered new papers and a clean disappearance by a sympathetic prosecutor, Tamsin instead makes his choice: testify under his birth name, resurrecting the identity he buried. The beat: identity reclaimed; invisibility refused.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, public for the first time. On the stand in Frankfurt, he speaks his real name aloud and walks the court through the ledger, dismantling the syndicate brick by brick while Kessler watches from the gallery, memorizing his face. The beat: courage with consequences; truth as both shield and target.

chapters.title: Brightwater
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Tamsin's POV. Months later, living openly if warily, Tamsin visits Voss's grave and pays back the favor that never happened—with interest—by funding protection for future whistle-blowers. Somewhere, Kessler's phone lights up with his address. The beat: bittersweet resolution; the price of survival was paid, and it was worth it.
